slides.narration: In Book III, Chapter 13, treat 13.1.1 Distinguishing Directed and Undirected Graphs as an algorithmic claim. A directed edge from u to v permits movement or dependency in one direction. The reverse edge is a separate fact. An undirected edge represents a symmetric relationship, so an adjacency-list representation usually stores it in both endpoint lists. A topological dependency ordering also makes sense only with an appropriate directed acyclic relation, not with every graph-shaped dataset. slides.title: 13.2.1 Building Adjacency Matrices
keyPoints: An adjacency matrix has one cell for each ordered pair of vertices, requiring O(V²) cells even when there are few.
Endpoint-pair lookup is direct indexing once bounds are checked.
Enumerating a vertex’s neighbors scans its row and therefore takes O(V), including absent entries.
An adjacency matrix has one cell for each ordered pair of vertices, requiring O(V²) cells even when there are few.
slides.narration: In Book III, Chapter 13, treat 13.2.1 Building Adjacency Matrices as an algorithmic claim. An adjacency matrix has one cell for each ordered pair of vertices, requiring O(V²) cells even when there are few edges. Endpoint-pair lookup is direct indexing once bounds are checked. Enumerating a vertex’s neighbors scans its row and therefore takes O(V), including absent entries. An undirected matrix is symmetric when its edge semantics are symmetric. The diagonal can contain self-loops; do not force it to zero or absent without a domain rule. A boolean matrix is enough only when weights and multiplicity are irrelevant. The conversion here collapses parallel edges by selecting the smallest weight. That policy is useful for some cost problems but loses multiplicity and all larger parallel weights. It is not a reversible serialization of the adjacency lists. The conversion allocates V² optional cells, initializes them as absent, then examines each stored edge: O(V²+E) time and O(V²) additional space, counting stored adjacency entries. At a graduate level, the answer is never just that the code ran.
